hook: A food truck sells three items on two days. A table of how many it sold, times a list of prices, gives each day's revenue in one step. That rectangular table is a matrix, and the "row times column" rule for multiplying matrices is exactly the arithmetic the food truck owner would do by hand.

prereq.why: Adding the equations gives $2x = 6$, so $x = 3$ and $y = 2$.

figure.caption: Each entry of a product is a row of the first matrix times a column of the second: $2(4) + (-1)(1) = 7$ goes in row 1, column 2.

chain.cause: A matrix has $m$ rows and $n$ columns
chain.effect: its dimensions are $m \times n$, rows first

chain.cause: The number of columns of $A$ equals the number of rows of $B$
chain.effect: $AB$ is defined; an $m \times n$ times an $n \times p$ gives an $m \times p$

chain.cause: Take row $i$ of $A$ and column $j$ of $B$
chain.effect: multiply matching entries and add: that is the entry in row $i$, column $j$ of $AB$

chain.cause: Swap the order of the factors
chain.effect: $BA$ usually differs from $AB$, or is undefined at all

ideas: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers. An $m \times n$ matrix has $m$ rows and $n$ columns; $a_{ij}$ is the entry in row $i$, column $j$.
Add matrices of the same dimensions entry by entry; a number times a matrix multiplies every entry.
Matrix multiplication: entry $(i, j)$ of $AB$ is row $i$ of $A$ times column $j$ of $B$, multiplied entry by entry and added. It needs columns of $A$ = rows of $B$.
Order matters: usually $AB \ne BA$. The identity $I = \left[ \begin{matrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{matrix} \right]$ gives $AI = IA = A$.

misconception.wrong: To multiply two matrices, multiply the entries in the same positions.
misconception.right: Each entry of the product combines a whole row with a whole column. Multiplying matching positions is a different operation, and it does not give the revenue, the combined transformation or anything else the product is used for.

summary: A matrix is a rectangle of numbers with dimensions rows by columns. Matrices of the same size add entry by entry. A product $AB$ is defined when $A$ has as many columns as $B$ has rows; each entry is a row of $A$ times a column of $B$. The order of the factors matters.
